title: Shopping at the Souq
description: Buying by the kilo in Sanaa's salt market: asking the price, counting to a hundred, saying it's too much and getting the seller to come down — plus when not to bargain at all.
approach: GPA Phase 2–3 — a bargaining exchange is heard whole, then rebuilt line by line; the number rules are noticed from the prices before they are stated.
unlock_condition: ≥11/15 on the price-and-number quiz and a recorded bargaining exchange with at least four turns
can_do: Buy something and ask the price
Count from eleven to a hundred
Say expensive, cheap and ask for a discount

grammar.title: Counting things: 3–10 plural, 11 and up singular
grammar.explanation: One and two come after the noun and agree with it: ولد واحد، بنت واحدة, and 'two' is usually just the dual ending -ayn: كيلوين، ريالين. Three to ten go before the noun and the noun is plural: ثلاثة جهّال. From eleven upwards the noun goes back to singular: عشرين كيلو, مية ريال. Money is the exception even under ten — it stays singular: خمسة ريال. The teens end in -aʿsh (حداعش، ثناعش، ثلاثطعش) and the tens in -iin (عشرين، ثلاثين، أربعين… تسعين); 'twenty-one' is واحد وعشرين, one-and-twenty.

grammar.title: How much? بكم and كم
grammar.explanation: Price is asked with بكم — 'for how much?' — before or after the thing: بكم ذا؟ الكيلو بكم؟ The answer uses the same بـ: الكيلو بمية ريال, 'the kilo is for a hundred riyals'. Plain كم asks a quantity: كم كيلو تشتي؟ 'how many kilos do you want?' — and the noun after كم is singular.

examples.english: A kilo is a hundred riyals
How many kilos do you want?

culture.title: The bargaining script
culture.note: In the open market the first price is an opening bid, and paying it marks you as a tourist. Ask بكم, react to the answer — a smile and كثير, 'that's a lot' — then offer about two thirds. The seller counters; you ask him to come down (نقّص لي); he names his 'last price'; you either accept or start to walk away, which often brings the price down once more. Keep it good-humoured and short. Do not bargain for bread, at fixed-price supermarkets, in a pharmacy, or over a taxi fare you already agreed. Qat, on the other hand, is bargained hard.

phrases.english: Too much! Knock a bit off

culture.title: Sanaa's markets and small change
culture.note: Old Sanaa's سوق الملح is a maze of specialised lanes — spices, silver, raisins, cloth — and the qat market fills every afternoon. Vegetables are sold by the kilo, spices by the handful. Riyal notes come in large denominations and sellers are often short of change, so keep small notes and expect باقي to be a negotiation of its own. Rounding down a few riyals for a regular customer is normal; tipping a market seller is not.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa also shortens this to أشري, and the past is شريت (Lesson 8). 'I want to buy' is أشتي أشتري — two verbs in a row, both bare.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman handing riyal notes to a vegetable seller over a pile of tomatoes.

example.arabic: أشتري خبز كل يوم من الدكان
example.transliteration: ashtari khubz kull yawm min id-dukkaan
example.english: I buy bread every day from the shop

vocabulary.video_hint: Grocery hauls and market walks: 'I'm buying…', 'I bought…'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Given in the 'he' form because it is the seller who sells. The seller himself is بيّاع. Final ع — feel it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A seller behind a stall of onions and peppers, weighing a bag on a hand scale.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vendor described or filmed selling; 'what do you sell?' in interviews.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Also 'dear' in the sense of beloved, so calling a friend غالي is a compliment. Feminine غالية. The bargaining word par excellence.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopper's shocked face at a large handwritten price tag.

example.english: The price is high, lower it for me

vocabulary.video_hint: Price reactions in market videos; 'everything is expensive' complaints.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The pair of غالي. خ then a long ii then the emphatic ص. A seller will insist his goods are رخيص before you have said a word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A heap of tomatoes with a small price card and a smiling seller.
vocabulary.video_hint: Sellers advertising low prices; comparisons of markets.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The noun you see on shop signs. In the market you do not ask for a خصم, you tell the seller to نقّص (lower it) — see the next words. تخفيض is the formal sign-word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shop window with a big red sign and a percentage on it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Sale signs; a shopkeeper offering a reduction.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Everything fresh is sold by the kilo. The dual كيلوين, 'two kilos', is the form you will use most. نص كيلو for half.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand scale with a one-kilo weight on one side and tomatoes on the other.
vocabulary.video_hint: Weighing at a market stall; 'a kilo of…' in shopping lists.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A plastic or paper bag from a shop; a handbag or suitcase is شنطة. Plural أكياس. Ask for a big one: كيس كبير.
vocabulary.image_scene: A black plastic bag full of vegetables being handed over a counter.
vocabulary.video_hint: Bags being filled and handed over at a stall or shop.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Plural أسعار — 'prices have gone up' is the national conversation. آخر سعر, 'last price', is the closing move in bargaining.
vocabulary.image_scene: A chalkboard of prices hanging above a vegetable stall.

example.english: The price is too much, lower it a bit

vocabulary.video_hint: 'Prices' in news-style vlogs and market reports.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The corner shop; plural دكاكين. محل is a bigger or newer shop, بقالة a grocery. Doubled ك and long aa.
vocabulary.image_scene: A small open-fronted shop stacked with tins, biscuits and water bottles, the owner at the counter.

example.english: The shop is in front of the mosque

vocabulary.video_hint: Corner-shop scenes; 'I'll go to the shop'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first of the tens; all end in -iin. Units come first: واحد وعشرين, خمسة وعشرين. The noun after any of them is singular.
vocabulary.image_scene: A twenty-riyal note laid flat with the numeral large.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Written مية or مئة, said miya. Before a noun it grows a t: مية ريال is said miyat ryaal. Two hundred is ميتين; three hundred ثلاثمية.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hundred-riyal note beside a row of ten ten-riyal coins.

example.english: A kilo is a hundred riyals

vocabulary.video_hint: Prices in the hundreds — the usual range for a kilo of vegetables.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Doubled emphatic ص; the MSA نصف loses its ف. نص كيلو, and later the time: الساعة ثنتين ونص.
vocabulary.image_scene: A watermelon cut cleanly in half on a market table.

example.english: I want half a kilo of tomatoes

vocabulary.video_hint: 'Half a kilo' at a stall; 'half past' in time talk.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'the remaining'. Hard g. Also 'the rest' of anything. Small coins are فكّة; خلّي الباقي is 'keep the change'.
vocabulary.image_scene: Coins and a small note being handed back across a counter.
vocabulary.video_hint: Change being counted out; a joke about no change.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Not a verb but a state: 'I am needing'. Feminine محتاجة. لازم لي does the same job: لازم لي كيلو بصل.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopping list in Arabic held up in a market lane.

example.english: I need a kilo of onions

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa keeps the ث: kathiir, not kitiir. After a price it means 'too much'; after a noun, 'many'; after an adjective, 'very'. The bargaining reaction.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopper holding up both hands at a price, eyebrows raised.
vocabulary.video_hint: Reactions to prices; 'a lot of people' in crowd scenes.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The command the buyer says: make it less. Hard g doubled, emphatic ص. Add لي: نقّص لي, 'come down for me'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A buyer's hand gesturing downward over a price card.

example.english: Knock a bit off for me, hajji

vocabulary.video_hint: The bargaining turn where the buyer asks for less.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends the bargaining. Either side says it: the seller to close, the buyer to ask for the real number. آخر كلام, 'last word', is the same move.
vocabulary.image_scene: A seller holding up fingers for a number with a 'final' expression.
vocabulary.video_hint: The closing turn of a haggle.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.arabic: السلام عليكم يا حاج، بكم كيلو الطماط؟
dialogue.transliteration: is-salaam ʿalaykum ya ḥaaj, bikam kiilo ṭ-ṭamaaṭ?
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you, hajji — how much is a kilo of tomatoes?

dialogue.speaker: Abu Saleh
dialogue.english: And upon you. Six hundred a kilo.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Saleh
dialogue.english: This is local tomato, it's not cheap.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.english: Come down a bit. I'll buy two kilos.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Saleh
dialogue.english: Fine, last price: two kilos for a thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Abu Saleh
dialogue.english: Here you are — and here's your change.

sound_spotlight.explanation: A doubled hard g followed by an emphatic ṣ. The whole word is low and heavy; that heaviness is what makes it sound like a real request.
One syllable, the y sliding straight into a long aa. Two syllables (ri-yaal) is the MSA reading.
'Hundred' grows a t before the noun it counts, like غرفة did before النوم. Listen for it in ستمية and ثلاثمية too.

lesson_sequence.detail: Nadia and Abu Saleh's exchange plays through once with pictures of the stall; the learner only listens.
Shopping words on cards with audio and picture; then the numbers 11–100 on a price board, tapped and heard.
Hear a number, tap the right form of the noun (جاهل/جهّال, كيلو/كيلوين). The rule appears after the drill.
See a price tag, say the question and the answer with بكم and بـ.
Role-play against Abu Saleh: the app plays the seller, the learner must use كثير، نقّص لي and آخر سعر before accepting.
Counter rolls up; nudge to price three things in riyals tomorrow.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you buy anything, ask بكم ذا؟ out loud — even at a fixed-price shop — and say the number back in Arabic.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on completion. Activates بكم and the numbers.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Convert three prices you see today into riyals and say them: ميتين، خمسمية، ألف.
At a real market, try one round of bargaining with كثير and نقّص لي — then accept the last price with خلاص.

video_needs.scene: A market walk-through with prices asked and answered on camera — a kilo weighed, a price disputed, change handed over.
